title: Hospitality and service standards
lead: What the Certified service practical looks like, how it's scored, and the Court's standards for demeanor, solving problems and dress.

intro.title: THE THIRD EXAM
intro.text: From Level 1: you watched formal service. At Certified you perform it, in a mock restaurant, and it's one of three parts you must pass the same day.

sections.name: The service exam, start to finish

lines.label: The day
lines.text: The Certified exam is one day with three parts: tasting, theory and a hospitality and service practical. You need 60% on each part, all at the same sitting.

lines.label: The practical
lines.text: It runs about 16 minutes and is set up like a real restaurant. The Master Sommeliers keep the time.

know: Arrive 10 to 15 minutes before your assigned time.
An Advanced Sommelier plays the Maître d': checks your opener, pen and notepad, then walks you in.
The exam starts when the Maître d' starts talking. The instructions are part of the test.
No phones or devices for notes. Underliners, serviettes and other tools are provided.
Usually one Master Sommelier sits at the table and plays a full table of guests.

sections.name: How the practical is scored

lines.label: The standard
lines.text: The Court's Hospitality and Service Standards are what candidates are measured against. They are formal on purpose.

lines.label: Three groups
lines.text: The Court's example feedback report scores hospitality and salesmanship, mechanics, and theory.

know: Hospitality is scored on confidence, gracious carriage and hospitality.
Salesmanship is scored on appetizing description and salesmanship.
Opening is scored on a confident, quiet, safe opening, the presentation and wiping the bottle lip.
Pouring is scored on correct glassware, clockwise service, no drips, the host taste, pace and pour height.
Order taking (repeat it, track it) and traywork (pace, carrying stemware) are scored too.

lines.label: Questions
lines.text: Examiners ask theory while you work: producers, vintages, classified growths, cocktails and other drinks.

know: A recommendation needs producer, vintage and full appellation for full marks.
Say why a pairing works, in words a guest would enjoy.
Know the top cuvées of top Champagne houses and the First and Second Growths of 1855.
Know top vintages of the last 10 to 15 years for regions like Champagne, Barolo, Brunello and Left Bank Bordeaux.
Be ready to give a classic cocktail's ingredients, mixers and garnish.

sections.name: The right attitude

lines.label: Attitude
lines.text: Quietly confident, never arrogant. No job on the floor is beneath a sommelier.

lines.label: Team
lines.text: The sommelier leads by example and sets the tone of service in the room.

know: Hospitality comes first, whether or not the guests are drinking.
A good team member never lets another team member fail.
Treat vendors with respect: honor appointments and return calls and emails.
Teach the team with an inclusive spirit. Simplify without dumbing it down.
Don't intimidate guests or co-workers with obscure wine facts.

items.name: GUESTS
items.text: Welcome and comfortable, drinking or not

items.name: TEAM
items.text: Help wherever needed; set the tone

sections.name: Reading the guest

lines.label: At the table
lines.text: Smile, be genuine, and keep the attention on the guest, never on yourself.

lines.label: Rapport
lines.text: Watch how a guest answers, speaks and sits, and adjust. Work out how much help they want.

know: Answer compliments with brief thanks.
Describe a wine briefly and accurately: aroma, flavor, structure.
Don't make things up. Offer to find the answer.
Listen actively and confirm the order back to the guest.
Learn and remember guests' preferences.

items.label: DO
items.title: Keep it on the guest
items.text:
Smile and make eye contact
Listen, then confirm the order
Brief descriptors: aroma, flavor, structure
'Let me find out for you'

items.label: DON'T
items.title: Make it about you
items.text:
Lecture with obscure facts
Overwhelm with detail
Guess an answer
Draw attention to yourself

sections.name: When something goes wrong

lines.label: The rule
lines.text: The guest is always right, and their perception is your reality. Fairness doesn't matter; fixing it in the guest's mind does.

lines.label: The steps
lines.text: Acknowledge it, let the guest explain, listen, ask how to make it right, decide, and bring in help when needed.

know: A rejected bottle comes off the table at once, with an apology. Check it away from the table.
Flawed wine: offer another bottle of the same. Sound wine: offer the list again.
Never put the guest in the position of being wrong.
A spill: apologize, act fast, offer to pay for dry cleaning, and reseat the guest.
A wrong bottle or price on the check: bring in a manager and stay diplomatic.

sections.name: Dress and appearance

lines.label: The rule
lines.text: The Court awards and deducts no points for appearance. Dress for safety, the guest and efficient service.

lines.label: Inclusive
lines.text: No clothing is gender-specific. Religious and cultural dress and all hairstyles are welcome, and disability accommodations are supported.

know: Any safe, workplace-appropriate mix of pants, dress, suit, blazer, shirt, blouse and shoes works.
Avoid large earrings and loose hair: they snag, and hair can land in food or drink.
Avoid short skirts (they limit movement) and open-toed shoes (slips and dropped objects).
No strong perfume: it gets in the way of the guest's meal and your own tasting.
The Service Standards add: pressed, clean clothes, safe shoes and clean fingernails.

visuals.text: The Court neither awards nor deducts points on any exam for how you look.

mixups.why: The Maître d' (an Advanced Sommelier) checks you in and gives instructions. The Master Sommelier at the table plays your guests.
Flawed: offer another bottle of the same wine. Sound: offer the list again. Either way, the guest is never wrong.
No points for appearance. But the Court still asks you to avoid loose hair, big earrings, short skirts and open toes for safety.
Full marks need producer, vintage and full appellation, plus why the pairing works.

facts.fact: The Certified Sommelier Examination is a one-day exam with three sections: Deductive Tasting, Theory/Business of the Sommelier, and a Hospitality and Service Practical.
A candidate must score 60 percent or higher on each exam section; all three must be passed at the same time at the same exam.
Tasting exam: four wines (two whites, two reds) in 45 minutes. Theory exam: 45 questions in 38 minutes.
Theory exam: 45 questions to be completed within 38 minutes.

The practical service exam approximates a real restaurant; candidates show salesmanship and knowledge while doing tableside tasks, and may be asked to open still or sparkling wine, recommend cocktails, spirits or beer, and discuss food and wine pairing.

Arrive 10 to 15 minutes before your assigned time. A local Advanced Sommelier acts as Maître d', checks you have a wine opener, pen and notepad, and escorts you in. Exam conditions start as soon as the Maître d' begins speaking; their instructions are part of the test and may be written down. No electronic devices for notes; all other tools are provided.
The Service and Hospitality exam is about 16 minutes long; Master Sommeliers keep the time, not the candidate. A group of candidates takes it at the same time.
Supplies to bring: pen or pencil, a notepad for the service exam (no phones for notes), and a corkscrew (bring two in case one breaks). Underliners, serviettes and other service items are provided.
Generally one Master Sommelier sits at the table and pretends it is a real restaurant with a guest at every seat. Watch reaching over a guest's space.

Adjudicators are there to help candidates succeed; the service exam evaluates knowledge and skill and is not meant to stump you. If things go wrong or you don't know an answer, stay professional and keep the focus on excellent service.

The CMS-A Service Standards are the basis for measuring candidates in CMS-A exams. They are formal and not appropriate for many restaurants, but candidates must display mastery of demanding formal dining room skills.

The Court's example Certified feedback report scores Hospitality & Service in groups: Hospitality & Salesmanship (Confidence, Gracious Carriage, Hospitality; Appetizing Description, Salesmanship), Mechanics (Mise en Place: Other Equipment & Tools, Stemware; Opening: Confident, Quiet, Presentation, Safe, Wipes Bottle Lip; Order Taking: Repeat Order, Tracks Order Correctly; Pouring: Correct Glassware, Clockwise Service, No Drips, Offers Host Approval Taste, Pace, Pour Height; Traywork: Pace, Tray Carry with Stemware) and Theory (Wine and Non-Wine).

In the example report, the Theory part of the service exam covers Wine (Climate, Fortified & Sweet Wines, Grape Growing & Vintage, Label Terms, Appellation-Region, Producer & Proprietary Blends, Grape Variety-to-Region) and Non-Wine (Food & Beverage Pairing, Producers, Cocktails, Flavor-Origin, Food Knowledge, Other: Apéritifs, Digestifs, Liqueurs, Sake, Spirits).

Possible service scenarios: open sparkling wine and serve; open and pour wines by the glass; serve a wine flight; discuss pairings and why they work; choose a pairing from several dishes; recommend a wine for a dish including region, producer and vintage; recognize producers of top regions; recommend similar producers; describe ingredients, mixers and garnishes of classic cocktails; name producers of major beer styles, sake, apéritifs, spirits and liqueurs; recognize apéritif brands, their country and general flavor.
Classic cocktails the guide lists as examples include the Negroni, Manhattan, Old Fashioned, Margarita, Paloma, Mojito, Sidecar, Moscow Mule and others.

Theory knowledge asked during the service practical can include top producers in major regions, top cuvées of top Champagne producers, First and Second Growths of the 1855 Bordeaux Classification, and top vintages of the last 10 to 15 years for classic regions such as Champagne, Barolo, Brunello di Montalcino and Left Bank Bordeaux.
For full marks on a pairing, mention producer, vintage and full appellation, and say why the pairing works in a guest-friendly way.
You may not know every producer or wine asked; write it down, repeat, and confirm any orders given.

Attitude: a sommelier should be quietly confident but not arrogant; no job on the floor is beneath the sommelier; hospitality comes first whether or not guests are drinking; the sommelier is part of a team and aware of all service in the room.

Vendors (distributors, importers, brokers, winemakers) are treated respectfully; no profanity or abuse; use their time efficiently, honor appointments, return emails and calls; today's colleague or vendor could be tomorrow's employer.
Colleagues: a good service team member does not let another team member fail. The sommelier is a high-visibility service leader who sets the tone in the dining room.
Team education: share knowledge with an inclusive spirit; avoid intimidating guests and co-workers with esoteric wine information; simplify without dumbing it down.
Tableside demeanor: smile; be friendly, respectful, engaging and genuine; attention is always on the guest, never drawn to the sommelier; answer compliments with brief thanks.
Guest rapport: understand the guest's priorities, wants and needs; watch their response, speaking manner and body language and adjust; assess how much help is wanted.
Know the restaurant's beverage program, food menu and policies. Give brief but accurate descriptors (aroma, flavor, structure) without overwhelming the guest.
Do not make things up: if you don't know an answer, offer to get it as soon as possible.

Communication: eye contact as appropriate; be an active listener; clarify what the guest says, especially when confirming the order; learn and remember guests' preferences; relationships are built over time.
Dealing with problems: the guest is always right; guest perception is your reality; the only 'justice' is the problem resolved in the guest's mind, and 'fairness' does not matter.

Problem resolution steps: 1 recognize and acknowledge the problem; 2 engage the guest and ask them to express themselves; 3 listen actively and completely; 4 ask how it can be made right; 5 decide what can be done within the guest's expectation and the house's policies; 6 rely on other key staff when appropriate.

Rejected wine: apologize and remove glass and bottle at once. Away from the table, check the wine. If flawed, offer another bottle of the same wine; if sound, offer the list to choose again. Never put the guest in the position of being wrong.
Spilled wine: apologize, act at once to limit staining, assure the guest the restaurant pays for dry cleaning, and reseat them, or move them to the bar while the table is reset.

Wrong bottle or price on a check: bring in upper management; apologize and politely suggest the guest pays for the bottle they believed they ordered; if they refuse, bring in the maître d' or manager; be diplomatic. Pricing complaints: acknowledge the opinion and tactfully state the restaurant's pricing policy.

Dress guidelines: the Court does not award or deduct points on any exam based on appearance; no clothing is gender-specific; religious and cultural dress and all hairstyles are honored; reasonable accommodations for disabilities are supported.

Exam dress: professional appearance prioritizing guest safety, your safety and efficient service. Suggested: any safe, workplace-appropriate combination of pants, dress, suit, blazer, shirt, blouse and shoes. No excessive perfumes or odors that interfere with the guest or your ability to assess wines.

Per Department of Health guidelines, avoid large earrings and loose hair (snagging, hair in food or drink), short skirts (restrict mobility) and open-toed footwear (less protection, more risk of slipping and tripping).
Service Standards appearance: pressed and cleaned attire with comfortable, safe shoes; clean fingernails; no excessive perfumes or odors.

unverified: The 16-minute length, the Maître d' role and the one-Master-Sommelier table come from the Court's exam guide (7.2024); details can vary by exam.
Scoring categories come from the Court's example Certified feedback report (fictional candidate 'Neville Nebbiolo', 2026). The Court does not publish the points per category.
The exam guide says the results reception is about 5:30 pm on one page and 5:00-6:00 pm on another; not used.

court.outcome: The practical service examination approximates a real restaurant environment. Candidates are expected to demonstrate salesmanship and knowledge while performing various tableside tasks. Candidates may be asked to open still or sparkling wines, recommend cocktails, spirits, or beer, discuss food and wine paring options, and generally show ability as a restaurant sommelier.

read.where: The Court **does not award or deduct points for appearance**. Dress the way you understand professional hospitality, putting the **guest’s safety, your safety and efficient service** first.

stops.name: Wear
stops.text: Any safe, workplace-appropriate mix of **pants, dress, suit, blazer, shirt, blouse and shoes**. The Service Standards add pressed, clean clothes and **clean fingernails**.

stops.name: Avoid
stops.text: **Large earrings and loose hair** (they snag; hair can land in a glass), **short skirts** (they limit movement) and **open-toed shoes** (slips, dropped bottles).

stops.name: Scent
stops.text: **No strong perfume.** It gets in the way of the guest’s meal and of your own tasting.

stops.name: Welcome
stops.text: No clothing is gender-specific. **Religious and cultural dress and all hairstyles** are honored, and accommodations are supported.
